title: Exploring Antitrust and Platform Power in Generative AI
venue: 1st Workshop on Generative AI and Law, co-located with the International Conference on Machine Learning
extended_summary:
This paper examines antitrust and market-power issues in generative AI, focusing on how a small number of large technology companies may control key parts of the generative AI stack. The authors discuss how dominance can arise through access to data, top technical talent, financial resources, proprietary infrastructure, and influence over academic research, and they frame these issues in terms of competition and platform power rather than educational use or learning outcomes.

The article does not study an intervention, product, or educational setting. Instead, it offers a legal and policy analysis of the generative AI ecosystem, using examples such as Google, Microsoft, OpenAI, and Amazon to illustrate vertical integration and potential barriers to entry. It also situates the discussion in the context of US and EU antitrust law and the emerging EU AI Act.

The paper concludes that current generative AI markets are likely to remain concentrated because new entrants face major data, compute, talent, and funding constraints. The authors argue that regulatory approaches may unintentionally reinforce incumbent advantages and call for further quantitative analysis of relevant markets and platform obligations under digital regulation. No K-12 population, educational intervention, or causal evidence is reported.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a theoretical/position paper on antitrust and platform power in generative AI, not an empirical education study. It does not present a study design, sample, comparison, or outcome analysis relevant to K-12 interventions.
impact_tier_rationale: No educational intervention or student outcome is evaluated, so there is no measurable impact on learning, engagement, or efficiency to score.
